Topic: Edexcel IGCSE Physics 4PH1, Unit 7 – Fission and fusion (spec 7.17–7.26). Fission
and fusion questions appeared 15 times in Paper 1 and Paper 2 between June 2019 and
June 2025.

7.17 Nuclear reactions as a source of energy

Energy is stored in the nucleus of an atom – this is the nuclear energy store. Three
nuclear reactions release this energy:


  Reaction        What happens                 Where it is used

  Radioactive     An unstable nucleus emits alpha,    Smoke alarms, medical tracers,
 decay           beta or gamma radiation            heat in the Earth’s core

 Nuclear fission  A large nucleus splits into two       Nuclear power stations (e.g.
                    smaller nuclei                      Barakah, UAE)

 Nuclear fusion    Small nuclei join to make a larger     The Sun and all stars
                   nucleus


Key idea: in every case, energy is transferred from the nuclear store. Exam questions
often ask: “Which energy store decreases during nuclear fusion?” → nuclear.

UAE link: the Barakah power station in Abu Dhabi uses nuclear fission to generate about a
quarter of the UAE’s electricity.

7.18–7.19 Fission of uranium-235

Nuclear fission = a large, unstable nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing
energy.

Step by step:

 1. A slow-moving (thermal) neutron is fired at a uranium-235 nucleus.
 2. The nucleus absorbs the neutron and becomes uranium-236, which is very unstable.
 3. U-236 splits into two smaller nuclei (the daughter nuclei or fission products), for
   example barium and krypton.
 4. Two or three neutrons are also released, along with gamma radiation.
 5. Energy is released as the kinetic energy of the fission products – they fly apart very
    fast.

Example equation:

¹n + ²³⁵U → ²³⁶U → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3 ¹n + energy

Balancing check: the mass numbers (top) and atomic numbers (bottom) must add up to
the same total on both sides.

  Mass numbers: 1 + 235 = 236, and 141 + 92 + 3 = 236 ✔
   Atomic numbers: 0 + 92 = 92, and 56 + 36 + 0 = 92 ✔

Exam tip – finding the number of neutrons: add the mass numbers of the products,
subtract from 236, and what is left is the number of neutrons. (Tested in Jan 2021 P1R Q10
and Jan 2021 P2 Q2.)

Important facts to learn:

   The daughter nuclei are radioactive – this is why nuclear waste is dangerous for a very
   long time.
   The neutron must be slow. A fast neutron is more likely to bounce off or pass straight
   through.
   Energy appears first as kinetic energy of the fission products. This kinetic energy then
   heats the reactor core (thermal energy store).

Model answer (not an official mark scheme): “Describe what happens when U-235
undergoes fission.”

  A slow neutron is absorbed by a U-235 nucleus (1). The nucleus becomes unstable
  and splits into two smaller daughter nuclei (1). Two or three neutrons are released (1)
  and energy is released as kinetic energy of the products (1).

7.20 Chain reactions

Each fission releases 2 or 3 new neutrons. If these neutrons go on to hit more U-235
nuclei, those nuclei also split and release even more neutrons. This keeps repeating – a
chain reaction.

   Uncontrolled chain reaction: the number of fissions grows very fast → huge energy in a
   very short time → a nuclear bomb.
   Controlled chain reaction: on average exactly one neutron from each fission causes
   another fission → a steady release of energy → a nuclear power station.





chain reaction · 1 → 3 → 9 fissions

The number of fissions multiplies at every step. This is why a reactor must remove
neutrons to keep the reaction steady.

The mousetrap model (June 2021 P1 Q3): a table covered with set mousetraps, each
holding two ping-pong balls. One ball dropped in sets off one trap, which throws two balls,
which set off two more traps… the whole table goes off in seconds. Each trap = a nucleus,
each ball = a neutron.

Model answer (not an official mark scheme): “Describe how a chain reaction happens.”
(June 2023 P2 Q5)

  A neutron causes a U-235 nucleus to split (1). The fission releases two or three more
  neutrons (1). These neutrons are absorbed by other U-235 nuclei, causing further
   fissions (1), so the process continues (1).

7.21–7.22 Inside a nuclear reactor: control rods, moderator and
shielding

This is the most tested part of the topic. Examiners love a reactor diagram with the parts
labelled and ask: what does it do? and what is it made of?


  Part        Made of        What it does           Why it is needed

  Fuel rods     Uranium-235      Contain the nuclei that      Source of the energy
                               undergo fission

 Moderator   Graphite or       Slows down the fast        Slow neutrons are much
              water            neutrons released by       more likely to be absorbed
                                      fission                   by U-235 and cause fission

  Control      Boron or         Absorb neutrons           Controls the rate of fission
 rods        cadmium                                  so that on average one
                                                          neutron from each fission
                                                         causes another

  Shielding     Thick concrete    Absorbs radiation (gamma   Protects workers and the
              (and steel)         rays and neutrons)           public from ionising
                                                                   radiation

 Coolant     Water (or a gas)    Carries thermal energy      Heats water to make steam
                             away from the core           for the turbine


Control rods – how they change the rate

  Rods pushed further in → they absorb more neutrons → fewer fissions → less energy
   per second.
  Rods pulled out → more neutrons free → more fissions → more energy per second.
   Emergency: rods dropped fully in → the chain reaction stops.

Don’t mix them up! (June 2022 P2 Q5)

   The moderator SLOWS neutrons. It does not absorb them.
   The control rods ABSORB neutrons. They do not slow them.

Memory trick: Moderator = Makes them slow. Control rods = Catch them.

From nucleus to the plug (Nov 2023 P1 Q9)

nuclear store → kinetic energy of fission products → thermal energy of the core → coolant
heats water → steam turns the turbine → generator → electrical energy.

Barakah link: Barakah’s reactors use ordinary water as both the moderator and the
coolant.

Model answer (not an official mark scheme): “Explain the role of the moderator.” (June
2019 P1R Q2)

  The moderator slows down the neutrons released by fission (1) so that they are more
   likely to be absorbed by U-235 nuclei (1) and cause further fission (1).


7.23–7.26 Nuclear fusion and the stars

Nuclear fusion = two small (light) nuclei join together to form a larger (heavier) nucleus,
releasing energy.

Example: two isotopes of hydrogen join to make helium.

²H + ³H → ⁴He + ¹n + energy

(deuterium + tritium → helium + a neutron). Check: mass numbers 2 + 3 = 4 + 1 ✔, atomic
numbers 1 + 1 = 2 + 0 ✔. This is the reaction tested in Jan 2022 P2R Q5 and Jan 2023 P1R
Q5 (ITER).

7.24 Where does the energy come from?

The mass of the products is slightly LESS than the mass of the nuclei that joined. This
lost mass is converted into energy. A tiny loss of mass gives a huge amount of energy.

7.25 Fusion powers the stars

   In the core of the Sun and other stars, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium.
   This releases the energy that makes stars shine – light and heat reaching Earth come
   from fusion.
   Energy is transferred from the nuclear store of the star (June 2020 P2R Q5).

7.26 Why fusion doesn’t happen on Earth easily

    All nuclei contain protons, so they are positively charged.
  Two positive nuclei repel each other – this is electrostatic repulsion.
   To fuse, nuclei must get very close, so they must be moving extremely fast.
   Very high temperature (millions of °C) → nuclei have enough kinetic energy to
   overcome the repulsion.
   Very high pressure (density) → nuclei are squeezed close together, so collisions
  happen often enough.

   At low temperature and pressure, nuclei move too slowly, repel each other and never
   get close enough to fuse.

ITER (France): an international fusion reactor being built to test fusion as a future energy
source. It must heat hydrogen to over 100 million °C and hold it with strong magnetic
fields, because no material container can survive that temperature.

7.23 Fission vs fusion – the comparison table


                       Fission                        Fusion

 What happens     A large nucleus splits            Small nuclei join

  Typical fuel         Uranium-235                 Hydrogen isotopes (deuterium,
                                                            tritium)

  Starts with       A neutron being absorbed       Very high temperature and
                                                    pressure

 Products           2 radioactive daughter nuclei +   Helium (+ a neutron) – little
                     2–3 neutrons                     radioactive waste

  Releases energy?    Yes                          Yes (more per kg of fuel)

 Where it happens    Nuclear power stations, e.g.       Stars; experimental reactors, e.g.
                     Barakah                      ITER

 Used for           Yes                        Not yet – too hard to reach and
  electricity now?                                       control the conditions


Both fission and fusion: release energy from the nuclear store, change one element into
another, and the total mass of the products is less than the starting mass.

Model answer (not an official mark scheme): “Explain why fusion does not happen at low
temperatures.”

  Nuclei are positively charged and repel each other (1). At low temperatures they do
  not have enough kinetic energy (1) to get close enough to fuse (1).

What the examiners test most

 1. Control rods and moderator (7.21) – in 6 questions. Learn the table in section 7.21 word
   for word.
 2. Fission equations and counting neutrons (7.18–7.19) – in 5 questions. Practise
   balancing mass and atomic numbers.
 3. Fission vs fusion (7.23) – in 4 questions, usually as “tick the correct box”.
 4. Why fusion needs high temperature and pressure (7.26) – in 3 questions. Always
   mention positive charge, repulsion and kinetic energy.

Common mistakes and self-check quiz

Mistakes that lose marks


 ❌ Wrong                    ✔ Right

 “The moderator absorbs neutrons.”        The moderator slows neutrons. Control rods
                                        absorb them.

  “Control rods slow down the neutrons.”      Control rods absorb neutrons to control the
                                             rate of fission.

  “Fission is when atoms split.”                       It is the nucleus that splits, not the atom.

  “Fusion happens in nuclear power          Power stations use fission. Fusion happens in
  stations.”                                      stars.

  “Energy is released as heat.”               Energy is released as kinetic energy of the

 Self-check quiz

 Cover the answers. Try every question, then check.

 1. What type of neutron is needed to cause fission of U-235?
 2. Name the two types of particle (apart from energy) produced when U-235 splits.
 3. Complete: ¹n + ²³⁵U → ¹⁴⁴Ba + ⁸⁹Kr + ? ¹n
 4. What is a chain reaction?
 5. Name a material used for the moderator, and say what it does.
 6. Name a material used for control rods, and say what it does.
 7. What happens to the rate of fission if the control rods are pushed further in? Why?
 8. Why is the reactor surrounded by thick concrete?
 9. What is nuclear fusion?
10. Where does the energy released in fusion come from?
11. Why does fusion only happen at very high temperature and pressure?
12. Give one similarity and one difference between fission and fusion.

 Answers

 1. A slow (thermal) neutron.
 2. Two daughter nuclei (fission products) and 2 or 3 neutrons.
 3. 3 – because 1 + 235 = 236, and 236 − 144 − 89 = 3.
 4. Neutrons released by one fission cause more fissions, which release more neutrons,
   and so on.
 5. Graphite or water. It slows down neutrons so they are more likely to be absorbed by
   U-235.
 6. Boron or cadmium. It absorbs neutrons to control the rate of fission.
 7. The rate decreases: more neutrons are absorbed, so fewer neutrons cause fission.
 8. To absorb radiation (gamma rays and neutrons) and protect people outside.





                                                                                                                                  Page 9 of 10
Read page 10 as text
 Fission & Fusion – Flipped Learning Notes (7.17–7.26)


 9. Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy.
10. The products have less mass. The lost mass is converted into energy.
11. Nuclei are positive and repel each other. High temperature gives them enough kinetic
   energy to get close enough to fuse. High pressure makes collisions frequent.
12. Similarity: both release energy from the nuclear store. Difference: fission splits a large
    nucleus, fusion joins small nuclei (or: fission is used in power stations, fusion powers
    stars).
